analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of big oil companies' profits above $40 a barrel and rebates the money to consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Durbin with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a 50% excise tax on the windfall profits of integrated oil companies — profits on every barrel of crude oil sold above an inflation-adjusted $40 base price. Most of the money would go back to individual taxpayers as a $150 rebate in 2006 and continuing rebates, with a share funding the low-income home energy assistance program and the rest going to the Highway Trust Fund. It also created tax credits for automakers who build fuel-efficient vehicles. The bill never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers get a $150 rebate in 2006 and, in later years, a rebate set at 75% of the windfall tax revenue collected. Low-income households benefit from a dedicated trust fund for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance program. Highway and transit users benefit because the remaining revenue flows to the Highway Trust Fund, with 100% federal funding for projects and 18.5% routed to mass transit. Automakers investing in fuel-efficient vehicles get new tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, low-income households, and transit users

how_it_helps.text: Each individual taxpayer would receive a $150 rebate in 2006 and, in later years, a rebate equal to 75% of that year's windfall profit tax revenue, credited or refunded even for taxpayers with no tax liability.

7.5% of the tax revenue would go into a new Low-Income Energy Assistance Trust Fund for the LIHEAP program, available without further appropriation once LIHEAP's regular appropriation reached $1.8 billion.
The remaining revenue would be deposited in the Highway Trust Fund, with the federal government covering 100% of project costs and 18.5% of the funds flowing to the mass transit account.

Automakers would get tax credits — a 20% investment credit, a 30% fuel-economy achievement credit, and a 30% credit for research and development — worth up to $1 billion a year, tied to fleet fuel-economy improvements reaching 50% by model year 2015.

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies would pay the tax: 50% of the sale price of every barrel of crude oil above an inflation-adjusted $40 base. If companies passed the tax on to customers, drivers would pay more at the pump, partially offsetting the rebate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Integrated oil companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Economists have long argued that windfall profit taxes discourage domestic oil production; the industry points to the 1980 windfall profits tax, which was repealed in part for that reason. The bill tries to limit this by excluding oil from wells drilled after enactment, but the risk of reduced drilling and higher pump prices remains.

The $150 consumer rebate is small compared with the energy price increases that prompted the bill, and the LIHEAP transfer is conditional: the trust fund only pays out if Congress first appropriates at least $1.8 billion for the regular program.
The automaker credits are capped at $1 billion a year and allocated by the Treasury Secretary, so support for fuel-efficient vehicles would be limited and would sunset after 2015.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a direct transfer from oil company windfall profits to consumers, energy assistance, highways, and cleaner vehicles, and its carve-out for newly drilled wells moderates the classic objection that such taxes reduce domestic production. The honest trade-off is that some portion of the tax could show up in gasoline prices, and the rebate would only modestly offset energy costs. On the merits it leans clearly toward ordinary households, but it was never debated, so its real-world design questions were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on November 9, 2005, during a period of high energy prices, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

After the referral, the bill's only recorded actions were two entries of the sponsor's introductory remarks; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the Finance Committee or on the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies and their shareholders are better off, since no windfall tax was ever imposed. Because the bill had no cosponsors and never advanced, its loss was determined more by the committee's inaction than by an opposing vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies that avoided the tax

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining 14 months of the Congress.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled the bill for a markup or hearing; the referral was the last action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no partisan split is recorded; the only support was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of their profit on every barrel sold above an inflation-adjusted $40, though the tax is deductible and newly discovered oil is excluded. Their interest in blocking it ran against the public's interest in rebates and energy assistance funded by the tax.

The bill creates up to $1 billion a year in tax credits for factories and R&D for fuel-efficient vehicles, conditioned on fleet fuel-economy gains reaching 50% by 2015. The public benefits from the same fuel savings the automakers are paid to achieve.
Windfall tax revenue deposited in the Highway Trust Fund would fund road projects at 100% federal share, with 18.5% going to the mass transit account.
